summary: Roomcraft loads as a polished, open-sided 6×4 m Three.js living room with genuine perspective and floor-plan views. The four required furniture types are present, additional pieces can be added, selected, rotated, recolored, deleted, and dragged with snapping and collision warnings. Save/restore/reset and the 390×844 layout were exercised successfully. The only diagnostic issue was a nonblocking missing favicon; all core scripts and styles loaded.

runtime.reason: The page loaded successfully with the Roomcraft title, rendered WebGL room, and responsive controls. Reload completed without a blocking error. The sole console error was a favicon.ico 404; the network log shows the core CSS, application script, and Three.js modules loaded.

scene.reason: The room is a real, orbitable 3D scene rather than a static image: the isometric, orbited perspective, and top-down views show consistent geometry, depth, occlusion, furniture volume, cast shadows, and daylight materials.

checks.reason: Depth and geometry were inspected across three distinct views: the initial isometric view, a top-down plan, and an orbited perspective. Furniture occlusion and floor/rug relationships remain spatially coherent across the views.

The composition has a clear hierarchy, restrained daylight palette, legible typography, and distinguishable furniture materials. The 3D room, wall details, rug, shadows, and UI form a coherent visual system on desktop and mobile.

The primary UI was exercised through adding, selecting, rotating, recoloring, deleting, dragging, switching views, saving, restoring, and resetting. Each action produced an immediate scene change and clear status feedback.

Repeated invalid drags visibly showed a placement-blocked warning and retained the previous valid position. A later valid plan-view drag succeeded, view changes were reversible, and save/reload/restore and reset recovered the expected arrangements.

The 1440×900 and 390×844 layouts were both inspected. On mobile the view tabs, project controls, selected-piece panel, rotation/color/delete controls, snapping, and all four palette buttons remain within the viewport. Reload worked; console showed only a favicon 404 and the resource log showed the core app and Three.js modules.
The initial screen identifies a 6×4 m, 24 m² open-plan room and visibly contains a sofa, coffee table, armchair, and floor lamp. The ‘Add a piece’ palette exposes all four required furniture types.

Selecting the sofa produced an outline and exposed controls. An added armchair was selected automatically, rotated from 0° to 90°, recolored coral, and later deleted with a clear confirmation; the palette also added another sofa successfully on mobile.

Furniture was dragged in perspective and in floor plan. The snapping switch changed the HUD from ‘Grid 25 cm’ to ‘Free placement’ and permitted a smaller move. During furniture dragging the camera angle did not change; orbiting only occurred when the empty room was dragged.

Specified furniture remained inside the room through successful moves. Three attempted invalid perspective placements produced ‘Placement blocked — returning to the last valid position’ warnings while the selected armchair stayed at its last valid footprint; no visible overlaps remained.

The selected coral armchair and the complete edited arrangement were unchanged when moving between perspective and floor plan. Orbiting afterward also preserved the arrangement and selection while changing the viewpoint.

Save reported ‘Layout saved to this browser’ and created the localStorage key roomcraft.layout.v1. Deleting the armchair reduced the room to four pieces; after reload and Restore, the five-piece saved arrangement returned with ‘Saved layout restored.’ Reset then reported ‘Initial living room restored’ and returned the 6×4 room to its four initial pieces with snapping enabled.

At 390×844, the selected-furniture panel, rotate buttons, color swatches, delete action, snapping toggle, view tabs, project controls, and all four palette buttons are visible and reachable. Adding a sofa on mobile immediately selected it and kept the editing controls usable without precision camera work.

instruction.reason: All requested flows are present and coherent: furnished room and palette, selection/editing, drag plus snapping, collision feedback, two synchronized views, persistence and reset, and adapted mobile controls.

spatial.reason: Furniture scale and footprints read correctly inside the 6×4 m room; the room shell, floor patterns, shadows, occlusion, and orbit/plan viewpoints consistently support the planning task.

interaction.reason: Editing sequences, view changes, collision rollback, snapping changes, save/reload/restore, reset, and mobile editing all produced reliable and understandable feedback.

visual.reason: The warm daylight palette, restrained typography, clean side panel, furniture materials, shadows, and responsive composition form a purposeful and legible design.

stability.reason: Desktop, reload, repeated editing, save/restore/reset, and the narrow layout remained usable. No crash or missing core asset occurred; only a nonblocking favicon 404 appeared in the console.

limitations: The 390×844 result verifies responsive layout and pointer UI, not physical touch hardware or multi-touch behavior.
Keyboard focus traversal was not separately exercised within the 40-call limit; mobile controls were verified through their UI accessibility roles and screenshots.
A conflicting 90-degree rotation into an occupied footprint was not separately recreated; invalid drag feedback and rollback were directly observed.
Console output contains only a missing favicon.ico 404, which did not block loading or interaction. Network resources for the app and Three.js modules loaded from the local server.
